summary: At APEC, Carney courts Asian investment and says China ties are not Trump's top worry before meeting him; Ford pitches an Ontario-Quebec front against tariffs.
body: At the APEC summit in Shenzhen, Prime Minister Mark Carney told business leaders that Canada is "also a Pacific nation" and pointed to Shenzhen's growth from a fishing village into a tech city as an example of what building fast can do.[^3] He asked Asian countries, including China, to invest in Canadian projects such as ports and pipelines, saying "every port and corridor we build needs a partner".[^1] Carney was due to meet Donald Trump later on Wednesday. He said China is "not the top issue at all" for Trump, because Canada mostly sells China canola, pork, seafood, gas and oil, "not cutting-edge semiconductors".[^1][^2] Since US talks broke down in August, the US has put 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, and Canada has hit back with its own.[^2]

Carney also disputed Vladimir Putin, who arrived in Shenzhen saying Western sanctions on Russia were a thing of the past; Carney called them "very real".[^1] He said any trade deal with the US must be one "in the interest of Canadians".[^2]

Closer to home, Ontario Premier Doug Ford told a Montreal business audience of nearly 1,000 that Ontario and Quebec should work together against US tariffs. He said the two provinces make up 61% of Canada's population and 58% of its economy, and he called for lowering trade barriers between provinces.[^4] In Ottawa, the House of Commons continued debating the federal budget; the Conservatives argue the government is "spending more, borrowing more", but with a majority the government is expected to pass it.[^5]
differences: Carney presents trade with China as low-risk commodities that need not trouble Washington; Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro has accused him of trying to "play China off the U.S."[^2] On the budget, the government says it will bring growth, while the Conservatives say it means more borrowing.[^5]
